chapters.title: Chapter 3: Debt Funds, Bonds and Gold

lessons.title: Gold in Every Form: Jewellery, Gold ETFs, Gold Funds and Sovereign Gold Bonds

body.text: Gold is one metal with several tax personalities. The wrapper you hold it in decides the holding period, the rate and whether a gain can be completely tax-free.

children.text: Meenakshi, a 52-year-old school teacher in Madurai, owns gold the way many Indian families do: wedding jewellery, a few Tanishq coins, Gold BeES units bought through a monthly habit on Zerodha, Sovereign Gold Bonds from an original RBI issue, more SGBs bought on NSE later, and some digital gold on a payments app. Her daughter's college fees are due, and she needs to sell some of it. Which one should go first? The answer depends heavily on tax.

body.caption: Gold taxation by form, tax year 2026-27

cells: Digital gold on apps and platforms
Gold mutual funds and funds of funds (unlisted)
SGBs sold on NSE or BSE
SGBs redeemed at maturity by an original subscriber who held throughout
SGBs redeemed at maturity after buying on the exchange, or redeemed early with RBI

body.text: No form of gold gets indexation any more, and none gets the ₹1.25 lakh exemption, which is only for listed equity. The real differences are the holding period (12 or 24 months) and the one route to a fully tax-free gain: holding an SGB from original issue to maturity.

body.title: Same Gold, Different Clocks
body.question: Meenakshi has held each of these for 18 months and all are in profit. Which sale gives a long-term capital gain?
options: Gold coins bought from a jeweller
Digital gold bought on a payments app
Gold ETF units bought on NSE
Units of a gold fund of funds bought through a mutual fund app
body.explanation: Gold ETFs are listed, so they run on the 12-month clock and 18 months makes the gain long-term. Coins, digital gold and an unlisted gold fund of funds all need more than 24 months, so after 18 months their gains are still short-term and taxed at slab rate.

children.text: Physical Gold: Jewellery, Coins and Bars

Physical gold is a capital asset even when you wear it. It becomes long-term after more than 24 months, and long-term gains are taxed at 12.5% without indexation. Your cost of acquisition is what you actually paid, which generally includes GST and, for jewellery, making charges shown on the bill.

body.caption: Meenakshi sells 50 grams of 24-karat gold coins bought in 2020 (prices illustrative)

body.title: Meenakshi's Coin Gain
body.prompt: Meenakshi bought 50 grams of gold coins at ₹4,800 per gram plus 3% GST, and sells them six years later at ₹11,000 per gram. Ignoring other expenses, what is her long-term capital gain in rupees?

body.text: Exchanging old jewellery for new jewellery at a jeweller is a transfer of the old jewellery, even though no cash changes hands. The value the jeweller credits you, after deductions for purity and wastage, is your sale value. If the old jewellery was bought long ago, that exchange can create a sizeable capital gain.

children.text: Most family jewellery comes without purchase bills. For inherited or gifted jewellery, cost is the previous owner's cost, and the previous owner's holding period counts too, so the gain is almost always long-term.

If the jewellery was acquired before 1 April 2001, you can use its fair market value on 1 April 2001 as cost. Get a report from a registered valuer that estimates that value based on weight, purity and gold prices on that date. Without bills or a valuation, you risk your cost being treated as very low and your gain as very high.

content.text: Get jewellery valued and photographed when you inherit it, not when you finally decide to sell years later. A contemporaneous valuation is far more credible.

children.text: Gold ETFs and Gold Mutual Funds

body.title: Gold ETF vs Gold Fund of Funds

columns.label: Gold ETF
points: Bought and sold on NSE or BSE through a demat account
Long-term gains at 12.5%, short-term at slab rate
FIFO applies per demat account, with the contract note date as the purchase date

columns.label: Gold Fund of Funds
points: Bought through a fund house or mutual fund app, often by SIP
Long-term after more than 24 months, because the units are not listed
Long-term gains at 12.5%, short-term at slab rate
FIFO applies per folio, and each SIP instalment is its own lot

body.label: Gold ETFs Bought Between April 2023 and March 2025
body.context: Gold ETFs and gold funds briefly fell under the deemed short-term rule for debt-like funds. Since the specified mutual fund definition changed from 1 April 2025, sales from that date follow the normal 12-month (ETF) or 24-month (fund of funds) clocks, even for units bought in that window.

children.text: Sovereign Gold Bonds: Three Exits, Three Outcomes

markDefs.definition: A Government of India security issued by RBI, denominated in grams of gold, with an 8-year tenure, an early redemption option from the fifth year and 2.5% annual interest on the issue price. Tradable on NSE and BSE.

children.text: tracks the gold price, pays 2.5% a year on the issue price and runs for eight years, with an option to redeem early through RBI from the fifth year. Its interest is taxable every year at your slab rate. How its capital gain is taxed depends entirely on how you exit.

stats.label: Held from original issue to maturity
stats.context: Exemption under section 70 of the 2025 Act, from 1 April 2026 only for original subscribers

stats.label: Bought on exchange, held to maturity
Early redemption through RBI after year 5
stats.context: Not exempt, since the bond is not held to maturity

events.title: First SGB tranche issued
events.description: Redemption at maturity by individuals was exempt from capital gains, and transfers of SGBs could use indexation.

events.title: Indexation removed
events.description: Long-term gains on SGBs sold on the exchange became taxable at 12.5% without indexation.

events.title: Maturity exemption narrowed
events.description: The Finance Act, 2026 limited the exemption to investors who subscribed at original issue and held continuously until maturity. Secondary buyers and early redeemers now pay tax.

body.title: Meenakshi's Two SGB Holdings
body.scenario: Meenakshi holds 20 units of an SGB she subscribed to at original issue at ₹3,150 per gram, and 20 units of another tranche she bought on NSE at ₹5,000 per unit. Both are redeemed at maturity in tax year 2026-27 at ₹11,000 per unit. She has never sold any of them in between.
body.prompt: Work out the capital gains tax on each holding.
body.modelAnswer: Original issue holding: gain of 20 × (₹11,000 − ₹3,150) = ₹1,57,000. She subscribed at issue and held continuously to maturity, so the entire ₹1,57,000 is exempt. Secondary market holding: gain of 20 × (₹11,000 − ₹5,000) = ₹1,20,000. Since she bought it on the exchange, the maturity exemption no longer applies from 1 April 2026. It is a long-term gain taxed at 12.5%: ₹15,000 before cess. Separately, the 2.5% annual interest on both holdings is taxable at her slab rate every year; on the original holding that is ₹1,575 a year.

body.title: SGB Interest
body.textWithBlank: The 2.5% annual interest on Sovereign Gold Bonds is taxed every year at your ___ rate, even when the gain at maturity is exempt.
body.explanation: SGB interest is income from other sources, added to your income each year. No TDS is deducted, so you must report it yourself using your AIS or bank statement. Only the capital gain at maturity can be exempt.

body.text: Digital gold sold through apps and jewellers' websites is not regulated by SEBI or RBI. In November 2025, SEBI publicly cautioned investors that these products sit outside its regulatory framework and lack the investor protections of gold ETFs and other regulated gold products. For tax, digital gold is treated like physical gold: long-term only after more than 24 months, with short-term gains taxed at slab rate.

body.title: Tax on a ₹1,00,000 Gold Gain After 18 Months, 30% Slab (Cess Ignored)

cards.definition: Jewellery, coins, bars. Long-term after more than 24 months, 12.5% without indexation.
Listed units. Long-term after more than 12 months, 12.5%. No ₹1.25 lakh exemption.
Unlisted units. Long-term after more than 24 months, 12.5%.
From 1 April 2026, only for original subscribers holding continuously to maturity.
2.5% a year on issue price, taxed at slab rate, no TDS.
A transfer of the old jewellery. The value credited is your sale value.

body.title: Before You Sell Any Gold
steps: Identify the form: physical, digital, ETF, fund of funds or SGB
Check the holding period against the 12-month or 24-month clock for that form
Find purchase bills showing price, GST and making charges, or a valuer's report for inherited jewellery
For SGBs, confirm from your RBI or broker records whether you subscribed at original issue
If you are close to maturity on an original-issue SGB, compare selling now with waiting for the tax-free redemption
Report SGB interest every year even though no TDS is deducted

points: Physical and digital gold become long-term after more than 24 months; gold ETFs after more than 12 months
Long-term gold gains are taxed at 12.5% without indexation, and short-term gains at slab rate
Exchanging old jewellery for new is a taxable transfer of the old jewellery
From 1 April 2026, only original SGB subscribers who hold to maturity get a tax-free gain
SGBs bought on the exchange or redeemed early are taxed at 12.5% on long-term gains
SGB interest is always taxable at slab rate, and digital gold is unregulated and taxed like physical gold

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and is not tax or investment advice. Gold prices and SGB issue and redemption prices used are illustrative. Sections and rates reflect the Income-tax Act, 2025 as amended by the Finance Act, 2026, for tax year 2026-27. Check RBI and scheme records and consult a qualified tax professional before acting.
